Tokenizer fertility — the number of tokens a tokenizer requires to encode a fixed amount of semantic content — varies dramatically across languages, and this asymmetry is baked into a model's fundamental architecture before a single weight is trained. A sentence in Thai, Arabic, or Yoruba may consume 3–8× more tokens than its English equivalent when encoded by a BPE vocabulary trained on English-dominated corpora, which means those languages consume more of the fixed context window, incur higher inference costs, and critically, receive proportionally less "representational budget" per unit of meaning during both pre-training and fine-tuning. The central question is whether this token-level inefficiency is a root cause — not merely a correlate — of observed performance gaps on downstream tasks like reasoning, translation, and instruction following for non-English languages. Beginners tend to treat this as a preprocessing inconvenience; experts worry about something deeper: that high-fertility languages are undertrained in the loss-function sense because cross-entropy loss is computed per-token, so a model sees fewer gradient updates per semantic unit for those languages even when raw token counts are held constant across languages in the training mix. A further concern experts hold is that vocabulary allocation itself encodes a hierarchy — morphologically rich languages get decomposed into sub-morphemic fragments that destroy linguistically meaningful units, forcing the model to reconstruct structure that English speakers get for free as atomic tokens.

The situation is more complicated than either undertrained or overtrained, and the complication runs in opposite directions depending on what you measure. At the token level, the high-fertility language is overtrained in the sense that the model sees many gradient updates per sentence — every fragmented sub-morpheme generates a prediction target — but those targets are artificially easy because predicting the next byte-pair fragment of a partially-spelled word is a much lower-entropy task than predicting the next meaningful word in English. At the semantic level, the language is undertrained because the model encounters fewer complete thoughts, fewer full syntactic structures, and fewer coherent discourse units per training step; Ahuja et al. (2023, "MEGA" benchmark) documented that languages like Telugu and Bengali underperform English by 20–40 points on reasoning tasks despite non-trivial token presence in training corpora, consistent with this semantic starvation framing. The gradient signal is also geometrically distorted: a four-token fragmentation of one Arabic word means the model must propagate useful semantic information across four sequential softmax predictions rather than one, with each intermediate step potentially washing out or diluting the representation through repeated projection. Rust et al. (2021, "How Good is Your Tokenizer?") showed directly that tokenizer fertility correlates more strongly with downstream NLP task degradation than raw training data size does — meaning you cannot simply add more high-fertility-language tokens and expect parity, because the structure of the signal is broken. The deepest expert worry is that the model learns a spurious skill: it becomes very good at low-level character-sequence completion in the high-fertility language while never developing the kind of chunked, concept-level representations that drive strong reasoning performance.

The geometric shallowness hypothesis has empirical support: when you apply representational similarity analysis (RSA) or measure the intrinsic dimensionality of language-specific subspaces inside multilingual models like mBERT or XLM-R, high-fertility languages tend to occupy lower-dimensional, more anisotropic regions of the embedding space. Püttmann et al. and related probing work show that representations for morphologically complex, high-fertility languages cluster more tightly and with less variance across semantically distinct inputs — a signature of a model that has learned surface-level continuation rather than meaning-sensitive encoding. The cross-lingual transfer implication is severe: cross-lingual transfer in these models depends on the hypothesis that languages share a common representational spine, but if high-fertility languages are mapped into a compressed, low-dimensional subspace while English occupies a richer, higher-dimensional region, the "alignment" between them is structurally asymmetric — transfer flows well from English into the high-fertility language (English representations are rich enough to project onto the compressed space) but poorly in the reverse direction (the compressed representations lack the dimensions needed to fully activate English-side structure). Libovický et al. (2020) found exactly this directionality in zero-shot transfer experiments: models trained on English and evaluated on Arabic or Hindi via cross-lingual transfer outperform the reverse setup by margins that cannot be explained by data volume alone. The practical consequence is that multilingual models are not truly multilingual in a symmetric sense — they are English-centric models with lossy compression codecs for other languages, and any task requiring the model to reason in or generate from the high-fertility language hits the ceiling of that compressed representation before it hits any data-size ceiling.

Joint tokenizer-model training is a genuinely promising intervention but the evidence suggests it shifts the problem rather than eliminates it. Work on byte-level and character-level models — MegaByte (Yu et al., 2023) and ByT5 (Xue et al., 2022) — shows that removing the fixed vocabulary entirely does improve cross-lingual transfer for high-fertility languages, with ByT5 outperforming mT5 on several low-resource morphologically rich language tasks, but the gains are uneven and the compute cost of operating at byte granularity is severe enough that the model must be shallower or trained on fewer total tokens to fit the same budget, potentially reintroducing the semantic starvation problem through a different door. The more targeted approach — adaptive or language-balanced vocabulary allocation, as in the FOCUS method (Dobler & de Melo, 2023) or vocabulary expansion via embedding initialization for specific languages — does measurably reduce fertility disparities and improves downstream task performance, but probing experiments on these models still find that the representational geometry for previously high-fertility languages remains somewhat compressed relative to English, suggesting the training dynamics during pre-training leave geometric traces that vocabulary repair alone cannot fully undo. The deepest issue is that even if you jointly optimize the tokenizer, the training objective (next-token prediction) still weights all token positions equally, so a language that now has lower fertility gets fewer gradient steps per training corpus pass in absolute terms — you've traded geometric distortion for statistical underrepresentation, and the model still converges to an asymmetric geometry if the data mix isn't simultaneously rebalanced. There is also a chicken-and-egg problem: a jointly trained tokenizer requires the model to have already developed some representational structure to inform which token boundaries are semantically useful, but that structure is precisely what's missing for high-fertility languages early in training, so joint training likely helps most for languages with sufficient data density to bootstrap good representations quickly. The honest summary is that architecture and tokenization changes are necessary but not sufficient — the geometry reflects the combination of vocabulary design, data mix, and loss function, and fixing one without the others yields diminishing returns.

Semantically-weighted loss is a well-motivated idea and partial versions of it have been tested, though never cleanly under that framing for the cross-lingual geometry problem specifically. The closest direct analog is token-level loss weighting by surprise or informativeness: Ohmer et al. and related work on "predictability-weighted" language model training show that upweighting high-entropy, low-predictability tokens during training improves syntactic generalization, which is exactly what you'd want for sub-morphemic fragments that carry near-zero information once context is established. On the multilingual side, the most concrete approximation is curriculum-based or importance-weighted data sampling — Shaham et al. (2023) and work on TPT (Token-weighted Pre-Training) demonstrate that downweighting easily-predictable tokens accelerates convergence and improves low-resource language performance, with reported gains of 3–7 points on XNLI for mid-resource languages, though the geometry was not directly measured. A cruder but widely deployed approximation is simply masking or upweighting content words versus function words or sub-word continuations in masked language model objectives, which CANINE and some mBERT variants explored — these do shift the representational geometry toward more isotropic language subspaces, but the effect is modest because the weighting is heuristic rather than dynamically computed from true information density. The fundamental obstacle to a clean implementation is that "information density" is itself model-dependent — you need the model to estimate token entropy to weight the loss, but the model's entropy estimates are unreliable early in training precisely when the geometric biases are being established, creating a bootstrap problem analogous to the joint tokenizer issue. What has not been tested rigorously is whether a two-stage approach — train a small fertility-balanced pilot model to generate information density estimates, then use those estimates to weight the full training run — would produce measurably more symmetric cross-lingual geometry, and this remains an open experimental gap.

Muennighoff et al. (2023) found that continued pre-training of BLOOM on additional languages improved surface task performance but showed diminishing returns on reasoning-heavy benchmarks, suggesting the model learned new statistical associations without restructuring the underlying representational geometry — exactly what you'd expect if the hierarchy is load-bearing and frozen. The continual learning literature offers a parallel: catastrophic forgetting research shows that early-trained representations act as attractors, and later training nudges weights within a basin rather than moving to a new basin entirely; applied here, the English-dominant geometry from early pre-training defines the basin, and multilingual fine-tuning cannot escape it without learning rates and data volumes that would themselves cause catastrophic forgetting of the original capabilities. Quantitatively, probing classifiers trained on frozen intermediate layers of models that have undergone extensive multilingual fine-tuning still show significantly lower representational variance for high-fertility languages than for English — the fine-tuning visibly improves the final layer outputs without repairing the middle-layer geometry where abstract reasoning is believed to occur. The practical implication is that post-hoc multilingual adaptation — the dominant industry approach of taking an English-dominant base model and fine-tuning for other languages — may be architecturally incapable of producing true multilingual parity, and that the only real fix requires intervening at pre-training before the hierarchy crystallizes.

The ordering effect is real and underappreciated relative to the proportion effect in the literature. Work on curriculum learning for multilingual models — including experiments by Zhang et al. (2021) on mT5 variants and ablations run by the BLOOM training team — shows that models exposed to high-resource languages first develop attention head specializations and positional encoding biases tuned to those languages' syntactic properties, and subsequent language introduction must work within those already-committed architectural preferences rather than shaping them. The mechanism is specific: transformer attention heads that develop early appear to preferentially encode the phrasal constituency patterns of whichever language dominated initial training, and because attention patterns are reused across languages via shared weights, late-introduced languages are forced to express their structure through heads that were optimized for a different linguistic geometry — Arabic VSO order or Japanese SOV scrambling gets approximated through English SVO-tuned heads rather than learned natively. A striking natural experiment comes from comparing multilingual models trained on genuinely diverse early corpora versus those that began with English and added languages: the BLOOM model, which attempted language mixing from the start, shows measurably more isotropic middle-layer representations for its target languages than LLaMA-based models that were adapted post-hoc, despite BLOOM having less total compute. However, the ordering effect interacts with fertility in a compounding way that has not been cleanly disentangled: a language introduced early but with high fertility still establishes a compressed subspace, whereas a language introduced late with low fertility inherits the anchor language's geometry but at least doesn't degrade it further — meaning early introduction is necessary but not sufficient for geometric equity. The open question that makes this practically difficult is that "order" in large-scale pre-training is not a clean variable — data is shuffled across documents but the effective order of linguistic exposure is shaped by domain, crawl vintage, and deduplication decisions in ways that are rarely tracked or reported, making controlled studies almost impossible on production-scale models.

There is meaningful evidence for differential freezing rates across head types, though the multilingual framing of this question is newer than the mechanistic interpretability findings it draws on. Induction heads — the heads responsible for in-context pattern copying, identified by Olsson et al. (2022) as forming in a distinct phase transition around 2-4 layers in small transformers — appear to be among the earliest and most robustly committed structures, and because they are largely language-agnostic in function (copying is copying regardless of script), they freeze early but do not themselves encode linguistic geometry in a damaging way. Syntactic dependency heads, by contrast, show strong language specificity: Michel et al. (2019) and Voita et al. (2019) identified that a small subset of heads carry disproportionate syntactic load, and probing work on mBERT by Muller et al. (2021) shows these heads develop English-biased positional preferences that persist through multilingual fine-tuning — these are the heads where the geometric damage lives. Coreference and long-range semantic heads appear more plastic, likely because coreference resolution has enough cross-linguistic structural similarity that the heads can be retrained without destabilizing the model's core syntactic scaffolding. The targeted intervention idea has been partially tested through techniques like adapter layers, LoRA rank decomposition applied selectively to attention versus MLP layers, and "head pruning then reinsertion" experiments — Pfeiffer et al.'s adapter-based multilingual work shows that intervening at the attention layer level rather than full fine-tuning does preserve more of the original geometry while improving target language performance, with roughly 40% less representational degradation on source languages compared to full fine-tuning. The critical unresolved question is whether you can surgically retrain the syntactic heads specifically — perhaps by freezing all heads identified as induction or semantic heads and only allowing gradient flow through syntactic heads during multilingual adaptation — and whether the syntactic heads for a new language can be initialized in a geometry-compatible way rather than overwriting the existing English-biased structure.
